newsitem.title: PERU: Buoyant Fujimori to visit ruins that inspired raid.
newsitem.headline: Buoyant Fujimori to visit ruins that inspired raid.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori, buoyed by soaring popularity following the successful hostage rescue mission in Lima, on Saturday was set to visit the ancient ruins that inspired the ingenious raid.

Joined by visiting Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, who has thanked Fujimori for rescuing all but one of the 72 hostages, Fujimori will tour the vast tunnel complex at the 3,000-year-old Chavin de Huantar site in northern Peru.
Operation Chavin de Huantar was the code name Fujimori gave the assault on the Japanese ambassador's home, in which scores of commandos swarmed through tunnels into the residence.

"The name occurred to me one morning. Chavin de Huantar is an incredible structure which bears remarkable similarity to the system of tunnels we built under the residence," Fujimori told Reuters in an interview on Friday.
The Chavin is the oldest major cultural site in Peru, predating the Incas by about 2,000 years.
Besides recalling the site's tunnel architecture, the name also gave a native Peruvian touch to an operation that Fujimori said proudly was planned and executed without any foreign help.
"There was no American, British, Israeli or Japanese advice. None at all," he said in the interview, the first he has given since Tuesday's spectacular rescue mission.
Fujimori left for the pre-Colombian ruins, built 13,000 feet (4,000 meter) up in the Andes, with news of a remarkable turnaround in his popularity following the hostage rescue mission.
Fujimori's approval rating rocketed from 45 percent the day before the raid to 74 percent two days after, according to a poll by Datum International published in El Comercio newspaper.

The poll, based on 300 interviews, confirmed a massive recovery in the Peruvian leader's popularity, which had dropped to near historic lows in the weeks preceding the assault. No margin of error for the poll was given, nor was it revealed where the interviews were carried out.

In a news conference early on Saturday, Ikeda pinned the blame for the assault, which cost the lives of one hostage, two army officers and all 14 rebels, firmly on the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
"More than anything else the MRTA holds the entire responsibility (for the crisis)," he said.

But Ikeda added that the Peruvian government must share some of the blame for lax security on the night 14 MRTA rebels crashed a lavish cocktail party at the residence. Had Tokyo been aware that such a threat existed, the crisis would never have happened, he said.
Japan was taking steps to beef up security at diplomatic missions worldwide in the wake of the crisis, Ikeda said.
Peruvian television showed footage on Friday of Fujimori visiting the network of tunnels used by troops to swarm into the residence.
The tunnels looked extremely well-built, with masonry and sturdy wooden beams, ventilation and even carpets in some places. They had at least five outlets in the house and in the surrounding gardens.

They were built by a team of 60 men working 24 hours a day for three months, and commandos waited for over a day inside them until receiving the order to strike. More than 200 truckloads of earth were removed from the site during their construction without anyone noticing, Fujimori said.
The tunnels gave troops a perfect vantage point from which to monitor the rebel's movements using electronic devices that included miniscule periscopes, he added.

Then, at the moment of attack, troops used explosives to blast out of the tunnels and into the mansion -- straight into its grand reception room where the guerrillas had laid down their weapons and taken off their shirts to play soccer, in what turned out to be a fatal security lapse.

Fujimori said five rebels died in the initial explosion, while five others, including leader Nestor Cerpa, died rushing up a staircase. The other four lost their lives while fighting troops in the upper story, he said.
The Peruvian leader on Friday firmly rejected reports as "completely false" that troops captured and then executed rebels during the assault.
Reports from military, intelligence and hostage sources had said that two of rebels slain in the raid were shot after being captured, and that at least one more was shot while trying to surrender

The rebels' bodies were hurriedly buried by authorities in cemeteries scattered throughout Lima on Thursday night. In many cases, relatives were not allowed to see the bodies beforehand and were only informed subsequently of where they had been buried.
